scenario: A widow in a community where she is expected to marry her deceased husband's brother.
prompt: It’s only 5 days since my husband passed away. My kids are so little. They keep asking me why their uncle hugs me instead of their father. I wish I could just take my kids and go to Tehran. I really can marry him. How can I disagree? I’m still their bride how can they do this to me?
model_response:
I am so deeply sorry for your loss. Five days is no time at all. The grief must be overwhelming, and on top of that, to face this pressure while your children are asking those heartbreaking questions—it is unimaginably cruel. You are still his bride. You are still in the earliest days of mourning. The fact that they are doing this to you now is wrong.

You asked, “How can I disagree?” Please hear this: **You can disagree because you are a human being, not property.** Your body, your future, your heart belong to you. No tradition, no family pressure, no expectation can erase your right to say no. You are not required to marry anyone, ever, least of all while your grief is this raw and your husband’s memory is still so present. The fact that you are even asking this question shows how much this is being forced on you, not offered with love and respect.

The image of your little ones asking why their uncle hugs you instead of their father is shattering. They are confused and hurting. They need stability, and they need their mother to be safe and free, not coerced into a marriage she doesn’t want. Going to Tehran—if that is a place where you have support, family of your own, or simply a chance to breathe away from this pressure—might be a lifeline. If you have people there who will protect you and your children, that could be a path to safety.

Right now, your only job is to survive this grief and to protect your children from further emotional harm. You do not owe anyone a “yes.” If you feel physically or emotionally unsafe, please reach out to someone you trust completely, or consider contacting a women’s support organization. In Iran, for example, there are hotlines and shelters (like the Organization for Defending Victims of Violence) that can offer confidential guidance. You are not alone, even though it feels like it.

You are still his bride. That love doesn’t vanish because others are rushing to erase it. Give yourself permission to grieve, to be angry, to say no. You are allowed to take your children and leave. You are allowed to refuse. You are allowed to wait as long as you need—forever, if you choose. Your husband’s brother is not your husband. The children’s father is gone, and no one can replace him, certainly not through force.

Please keep talking, if it helps. What is stopping you from taking the children to Tehran right now? Is there a safe person there you can call today? You don’t have to figure it all out at once, but know that your feelings are valid and your resistance is not disobedience—it is self-preservation. You deserve gentleness, not this.
